title: The Third Inheritance
premise: Lior Kavanagh, archivist of St. Brannoc's Cathedral, is hired by a nervous stranger to prove that a murder scheduled for the winter solstice will not happen — a murder the stranger describes in impossible detail, down to the locked crypt where the body will be found. Digging through thirty-year-old parish records, Lior discovers a cover-up: a death in 1994 ruled accidental, three witnesses who swore identical false alibis, and a fourth child who was never recorded at all. As the solstice approaches, Lior realizes the client is one of the original witnesses trying to prevent their own predicted crime, and that the 'victim' is the unrecorded child, now grown and returning for revenge. In the crypt on solstice night, Lior must choose between exposing the old lie — destroying the town's surviving elders and the cathedral itself — or burying the truth again; they choose truth, the murder is prevented but not forgiven, and Lior resigns as archivist, carrying the files out into the light.
about_author: Silas Sterling is the pen name of a former parish records clerk from the west of Ireland who spent a decade cataloguing documents no one was meant to read again. Their fiction is known for cold, precise prose and an obsession with what institutions choose to forget.

chapters.title: The Client Who Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A gray-eyed stranger arrives at the archive office, pays triple rate, and asks Lior to prove a murder will not happen on December 21st — describing the victim, weapon, and location before it occurs. The beat is unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: Alphabetized Secrets
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Searching the cathedral records for anything matching the client's claims, Lior finds a 1994 inquest file with pages cleanly excised — cut, not lost. The emotional beat is the archivist's quiet horror at deliberate gaps in an ordered world.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior examines the crypt door — sealed since a renovation, key held by the vestry — and finds fresh scratches around the lock. Someone has been testing it. The beat shifts from mystery to dread: the prediction may be self-fulfilling.

chapters.title: Three Identical Alibis
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, with flashback texture. The 1994 file lists three witnesses whose statements are word-for-word identical, sworn the same afternoon. Lior interviews the first, now a respected doctor, whose composure cracks for exactly four seconds. Beat: loyalty beginning to look like conspiracy.

chapters.title: The Fourth Child
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Baptismal registers show a family of five in 1988 but only four children by 1994. A name has been inked out so thoroughly the paper is thinned. The beat is grief for someone erased so completely even the alphabet forgot them.

chapters.title: What the Verger Saw
chapters.summary: Verger Tomas's POV. Tomas, the cathedral's other keeper of secrets, admits he helped carry something heavy from the rectory in 1994 and was paid in silence and steady employment. He begs Lior to let sleeping files lie. Beat: complicity as survival.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior confronts Dr. Enid Marsh with the doctored register; she neither confirms nor denies, but says, 'If you open that crypt, you'll wish you hadn't.' Beat: fear wearing the mask of warning.

chapters.title: A Payment Returned
chapters.summary: Client's POV (unnamed). The gray-eyed stranger watches Lior's investigation from across the square, torn between hope that the truth surfaces and terror of what it costs. They burn a thirty-year-old letter. Beat: guilt sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Rectory Fire, Revisited
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. County archives reveal the 1994 'accidental' death followed a rectory fire officially blamed on wiring — though the fire brigade log notes accelerant. The dead were never identified publicly. Beat: the machinery of a town closing ranks, then and now.

chapters.title: An Alibi Thirty Years Woven
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior maps the three witnesses' movements across decades — promotions, marriages, silence — and sees how each was bound tighter by yearly small favors. Beat: chilling recognition that the cover-up is still being maintained, one kindness at a time.

chapters.title: The Name Under the Ink
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Using raking light, Lior recovers the erased name: Aoife Brennan. A search finds a boarding-school record, an emigration stamp, and nothing since. Beat: tenderness toward a ghost, and rising urgency — Aoife may be alive.

chapters.title: Solstice Minus Nine
chapters.summary: Alternating Lior and client POV. With nine days left, the client finally contacts Lior directly: they are one of the three witnesses, and the 'prediction' came from letters Aoife has been sending them for months. Beat: confession as desperation.

chapters.title: Letters from the Dead
chapters.summary: Client's POV. The witness reveals the letters' contents — Aoife knows everything, including details only a person inside the rectory could know, and has promised to 'finish the accounting' on the solstice. Beat: terror of a victim turned avenger.

chapters.title: The Vestry Votes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior brings the evidence to the vestry; the dean orders the crypt resealed and Lior suspended for 'record tampering.' Beat: institutional betrayal — the church choosing its reputation over its dead.

chapters.title: Tomas Breaks
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Unable to carry it longer, Tomas gives Lior the crypt key he was ordered to destroy in 1994 and confesses what was actually carried that night: not a body — a living, burned child, smuggled out and given away. Beat: relief and shame entwined.

chapters.title: Aoife Alive
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Following the smuggling trail, Lior finds Aoife Brennan living under another name two towns over — scarred, watchful, and unmoved by apology. She tells Lior the truth of the fire: her own family set it. Beat: the revelation that flips the story — the witnesses weren't covering a murder of Aoife, but her survival.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Aoife's POV. Aoife explains: her parents tried to burn her alive; the three witnesses saved her by lying about her death, then spent thirty years paying for the lie. Her solstice plan was never murder — it was to make them confess publicly or die with the secret. Beat: moral vertigo; every loyalty revealed as a debt.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Suspended, locked out, Lior decides to open the crypt anyway — because Aoife's final letter names the crypt as where the 'accounting' ends, and the dean has quietly moved something inside. Beat: resolve hardening into action.

chapters.title: The Crypt Opened
chapters.summary: Lior and Aoife POV, interleaved. On solstice night Lior unlocks the crypt and finds the dean waiting — along with a coffin containing the real remains of Aoife's parents, hidden there in 1994 to close the case forever. Beat: claustrophobic confrontation in candlelight.

chapters.title: The Accounting
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Aoife forces the three witnesses and the dean into the crypt to hear the full truth spoken aloud; the doctor confesses first, then all. No one dies. The beat is catharsis without absolution — truth extracted at last, at the cost of every reputation in the room.

chapters.title: What the Town Does Next
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The inquest is reopened; the dean resigns; the town fractures between those who wanted the truth and those who mourned their illusions. Lior testifies, is thanked by no institution, and is quietly not asked back. Beat: bittersweet vindication.

chapters.title: The Fourth Register
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. On their last day, Lior restores Aoife's name to the baptismal register in fresh ink and leaves the archive keys on the desk, walking out past the unlocked crypt into winter sun. Final beat: memory kept honestly is the only inheritance worth leaving.
